The certificate authority keeps the public keys, not the private keys. When you get data from them it's simply an acknowledgment that they verify that the said public key actually does belong to the company in question. The reason certificate authorities being hacked is dangerous is because it means the hacker can use that certificate authority's private key to create fake keys that seem to actually come from a trusted authority.

This is exactly what happened with the recent Lenovo installed adware. Lenovo included spyware on their laptops, but the developer of this spyware was particularly retarded. They wanted to inject ads into secure connections so what they did was add a fake trusted authority on your computer and then had YOU create the certificates on-the-fly which were then injected into sites you were visiting. You basically turned into the trusted authority. If all the above made sense you might be able to already figure out how hackers took advantage of this. Since you were the trusted authority that means the private key you were using to generate your certificates was right on your computer. Hackers took this private key and suddenly could remotely generate trusted connections. So a malicious third party could pretend to be anybody, for instance BankUSA, and create a 'secure' connection with anybody using a Lenovo laptop with their spyware still on it.

The TL/DR version of this all is that hacking a certificate authority means you can generate man in the middle attacks, not that you can decrypt third party traffic.

You've just described symmetric cryptography, this is why we use asymmetric cryptography now.
What are the benefits of asymmetric encryption? Is it more scalable?

With symmetric encryption, both parties use the same key to encrypt/decrypt. If that key is intercepted while both parties are sending messages to agree on what the key should be, their future communications can be decrypted.

With asymmetric encryption, you have a public and private key. The public key can be shared with anyone to encrypt data being sent to you. Only your private key can decrypt it, so that isn't shared with anyone else.

The only problem with asymmetric is it's a lot slower than symmetric. What lost of protocols do is use asymmetric encryption to encrypt the negotiation of a symmetric key. This ensures that the symmetric key is not intercepted and they can start using the faster, symmetric, key once parties agree on which key to use.

While I'm on a nitpicking roll, we still use symmetric cryptography for almost everything. It's very fast and very secure, the only problem with it is how to agree on the shared key. This is where asymmetric (public-key) cryptography comes in. We generate a random 'session key' and then use public key cryptography (which is too slow to be much use as a bulk encryption method) to exchange that session key. Then the rest of the session uses 3DES or Blowfish or whatever's fashionable these days.

That's symmetric encryption. With asymmetric, you have two keys: one to encrypt (public) and one to decrypt (private). You can share your public key with anyone who wants to send you data and, since only you have the private key to decrypt it, no one else can see what's being sent to you.

So over the past few days, I've tried Apricity OS (Still in Beta) and Antergos. Both had simple installers and were easily navigated via a new linux user. My machine is a toshiba satellite l650-06Q, with an i3 and 4GB ram.

We'll Start with Apricity. Apricity is an arch based distro that is geared towards persons who want to make an HTPC, or just have everything right at their finger prints. It uses a stripped down gnome DE that is meant to run light. For me, it booted into around 350mb of RAM. The people of at Softpeadia reviewed the OS just days ago going into much more detail.

All in all, it was a good experience. The only issue was that when trying to review the number of work spaces, I lost all the pre sets for gnome. I would recommend trying this distro out just to play with it. Although, final judgement cannot be rendered until they release a final product.

What hasn't been said about Antergos? Antergos came from the ashes of the Cinnarch program, but now offers 5 DE's. One of them being XFCE, who I am a fan of. The OS is more or less vanilla arch with an extra repository, and some pre loaded packages. I recently installed antergos on my nieces laptop and she is adjusting very well with it coming from Win7. She is a complete linux noobie, and it has been very stable for he. Trying it out on my laptop, it booted into ~250mb of ram. For more info, feel free to read a review by ORDINATECHNIC.

I will be installing Antergos full time to use for the next few weeks to give it a solid run. Also, Next week I'll following it and combine it with an added program list.

See you then!
